subject: Sapphire Analytics — selecting a connectivity path for on-prem private deploy
messages:
From: Tom Ellis <tom.ellis@sapphire-analytics.com>
To: kimberly_park@redwood.com
Cc: priya.r@sapphire-analytics.com
Date: 2026-07-26T09:03:00-07:00
Subject: Initial: connectivity options for Sapphire on-prem LLM deployment

Hi Kimberly,

Thanks again for the quick intro last week. We're getting ready to stand up a private Redwood deployment that will terminate in our on-prem inference cluster (colo) and also need to expose it to a set of AWS-hosted VPCs that run our ingestion and orchestration. Key constraints:

- Low tail latency for customer-facing inference (p95 target < 100ms)
- Strict data residency + audit trail requirements (SOC-friendly)
- Multiple AWS accounts with a shared Transit Gateway in our org
- Some of our edge sites use RFC1918 ranges that overlap with Redwood's default subnets
- Expected steady-state throughput ~ 800 req/s with bursts to 2.5k req/s

Can you recommend whether we should pursue VPC peering (intra-account and cross-account), PrivateLink (interface endpoints), or site-to-site VPN (IPSec) for the connectivity? We want a clear rationale (latency, operations, security tradeoffs) and any immediate blockers from Redwood's side.

I've attached a simple network diagram and a procurement checklist. Happy to hop on a call — Priya will be the technical owner for the infra side.

Thanks,
Tom 
Director, Platform Engineering
Sapphire Analytics

Attachments: sapphire-network-diagram.v1.pdf, sapphire-procurement-req.pdf

From: kimberly_park@redwood.com
To: Tom Ellis <tom.ellis@sapphire-analytics.com>
Cc: priya.r@sapphire-analytics.com, marcus_lin@redwood.com
Date: 2026-07-26T10:45:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Initial: connectivity options for Sapphire on-prem LLM deployment

Tom — thanks for the clear summary and the diagram; this is helpful. High level recommendation up front so you can plan: avoid a one-size-fits-all peering-only approach. For Sapphire's constraints I recommend we design for PrivateLink (interface endpoints) as the primary path for control-plane and model inference traffic where possible, paired with a dedicated site-to-site VPN path as an encrypted fallback for burst/failover and for environments where IP overlap prevents peering. VPC peering is attractive for raw throughput/latency but has operational limitations (no transitive routing, cross-account scale, and IP overlap risk).

Summary rationale (short):
- Latency: pure VPC peering will usually show the lowest hop count, but PrivateLink often has comparable p95 in practice and gives better isolation and easier cross-account access controls.
- Security & compliance: PrivateLink minimizes surface area (no open route tables), plus it keeps traffic within AWS control planes which simplifies audit trails. S2S VPN adds a clear encrypted link with good auditability for on-prem.
- Operational: Peering requires co-ordination per-VPC and fails on transitive routing — if you expect many VPCs, maintenance becomes heavy. PrivateLink + TGW/ALB fronting is easier to version and roll out.
- IP overlap: peering is blocked by overlapping RFC1918; PrivateLink and VPN can NAT/translate to avoid conflicts.

Immediate Redwood considerations:
1) We'll need to know whether you want to use an AWS Transit Gateway as the aggregation point (TGW + PrivateLink) or manage per-VPC endpoints.
2) For on-prem MTU and perf testing: VPN tunnels can reduce MTU and impact throughput; we'll want to run a short perf sweep during POC.
3) Our default connector supports PrivateLink and S2S tunnel modes; peering is supported in single-account pilots but we recommend PrivateLink for Scale.

Next steps I propose:
- Quick 45-minute working session with you, Priya, and our infra engineer Marcus to vet TGW vs per-VPC endpoints and confirm CIDR overlap remediation.
- Marcus to draft a short matrix (latency/ops/cost/security) with numeric assumptions for your expected traffic.

If that sounds good, I'll schedule the call and loop in Connor from our field ops for deployment runbook items.

Thanks,
Kimberly Park
Account Lead, Redwood Inference
kimberly_park@redwood.com
Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Initial: connectivity options for Sapphire on-prem LLM deployment

Tom/Priya — digging into the specifics. I built a short decision matrix below and included practical config notes. This is focused on the data plane (inference traffic).

Decision matrix (Sapphire constraints = Low tail latency, SOC audit, overlapping CIDRs, multi-account TGW):

1) VPC Peering
- Pros: Minimal encapsulation overhead, low latency (often best raw p95), simple routing inside single-account where IPs don't overlap.
- Cons: No transitive routing (can't use peering + TGW to reach all accounts), cross-account scale limited (per-peering setup), fails with overlapping private CIDR blocks, route table sprawl and potential human error.
- Ops: Each peering requires pairwise setup + route maintenance. No built-in private service audit trail beyond VPC flow logs.
- When to pick: small number of VPCs, no CIDR overlap, extremely latency-sensitive internal-only workloads.

2) PrivateLink (Interface Endpoints)
- Pros: Endpoint services terminate at ENIs under your account control, traffic stays within AWS fabric (good for audits), access controlled via endpoint policies, works well cross-account, avoids route table changes for consumers. Scales better operationally at multi-account level.
- Cons: Slightly higher per-request overhead vs raw peering due to proxying to the endpoint service; costs per-ENI and per-GB egress.  Limits on concurrent connections are usually manageable but need sizing.
- Ops: Versioned model endpoints can be published as PrivateLink services; easier to rollback. Observability: we can surface per-endpoint metrics.
- When to pick: multi-account orgs, need auditability and fine-grained access control, or when CIDR overlap is present.

3) Site-to-Site VPN (IPSec)
- Pros: Clear encrypted tunnel for on-prem to cloud, works across CIDR overlaps with NAT, vendor-agnostic, straightforward for regulatory auditors. Can be used as primary for on-prem and PrivateLink as a cloud-to-cloud fallback.
- Cons: MTU issues, variable latency depending on colo egress, throughput limited by tunnel endpoints and CPU unless you use hardware VPN/Direct Connect. BGP flaps and churn need ops attention.
- Ops: Good for durable, audited connectivity. Plan HA with dual tunnels/paths.
- When to pick: on-prem primary path, audits require explicit external encryption, or CIDR overlap that can't be reconciled.

Recommended config for Sapphire (practical):
- Primary: PrivateLink service for inference endpoints exposed per-region (frontend) + TGW in your org to aggregate VPCs if you want centralized routing and security controls. PrivateLink gives the clean cross-account model.
- Fallback/On-prem: A pair of HA site-to-site VPN tunnels from your colo to a dedicated VPC that hosts the PrivateLink consumer ENIs. Use NAT for CIDR overlap cases.
- Avoid: wide-scale VPC peering across many accounts — causes operational sprawl and is fragile for overlapping netblocks.

Sizing & perf notes:
- For your 800 req/s steady, 2.5k bursts: size PrivateLink ENIs across at least 3 AZs and validate concurrent connections. We should bench with a 2x safety factor.
- For VPN: test effective throughput at expected payload sizes (token response sizes) — IPSec tunnels can bottleneck on CPU; consider a hardware crypto appliance or using AWS VPN/Direct Connect when sustained bandwidth matters.
- MTU: ensure jumbo frames/end-to-end MTU compatibility; plan for ~1400 path MTU for IPsec without fragmentation by default.

Operational items for us to prepare:
- We'll produce the matrix as an XLS with numeric latency assumptions and estimated costs (I'll attach next).
- Need your TGW topology: do you prefer a central TGW under your network account or per-product TGWs? That drives whether we centralize PrivateLink consumers.
- Confirm whether overlapping CIDRs can be renumbered for any of the VPCs — even partial renumbering reduces complexity.

I'll attach the connector sizing matrix and a short checklist in the follow-up. If we all agree on PrivateLink + S2S fallback, Connor can draft the deployment runbook.

— Marcus Lin
Principal Infra Engineer, Redwood Inference
marcus_lin@redwood.com

Kim/Marcus/Connor — thanks, this is exactly the level of detail we needed. We reviewed internally and agree to proceed with the PrivateLink-primary + S2S VPN fallback pattern. Action items from our side:

- Procurement: I attached the procurement PDF with a request for a second HA VPN endpoint and an AWS support request ticket number.
- TGW: we'll use our central TGW and will delegate a consumer attachment for the Redwood consumer VPC.
- CIDR: we can renumber one non-prod VPC but will need NAT for prod due to constraints.

Next steps agreed:
1) Schedule the 45-minute design call (please propose times).
2) Marcus to send the connector sizing spreadsheet (redwood-connector-matrix.xlsx) + estimated costs.
3) Connor to draft a deployment runbook with cutover checklist.

We're aiming for a POC in the next 3 weeks. Thanks again — Priya and I will be on the design call.

Best,
Tom
